import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1136

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1136](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1136)
- [Mu11] Müller, Helmut, *Über ein additiv-zahlentheoretisches Problem von P. Erdős*.
  Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamburg (2011), 75-78.
-/

namespace Erdos1136

/--
A set `A` of natural numbers has the property in the question if `a + b ≠ 2 ^ k` for all
`a, b ∈ A` (not necessarily distinct) and all `k ≥ 0`.
-/
def AvoidsPowersOfTwo (A : Set ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ A, ∀ b ∈ A, ∀ k : ℕ, a + b ≠ 2 ^ k

/-- The set of all integers congruent to $3\cdot 2^i\pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for some $i\geq 0$. -/
def muellerSet : Set ℕ := {n | ∃ i : ℕ, n ≡ 3 * 2 ^ i [MOD 2 ^ (i + 2)]}

/--
Does there exist $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with lower density $>1/3$ such that $a+b\neq 2^k$ for
any $a,b\in A$ and $k\geq 0$?

Müller [Mu11] settled this question in the affirmative: in fact one can take $A$ to be
the set of all integers congruent to $3\cdot 2^i\pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for any $i\geq 0$, which has
density $1/2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1136.lean"]
theorem erdos_1136 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ A : Set ℕ, (1 / 3 : ℝ) < A.lowerDensity ∧ AvoidsPowersOfTwo A := by
  sorry

/--
Achieving density $1/3$ is trivial, taking $A$ to be all multiples of $3$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1136.variants.multiples_of_three :
    AvoidsPowersOfTwo {n : ℕ | 3 ∣ n} ∧ Set.HasDensity {n : ℕ | 3 ∣ n} (1 / 3) := by
  sorry

/--
Müller [Mu11] settled this question in the affirmative: in fact one can take $A$ to be
the set of all integers congruent to $3\cdot 2^i\pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for any $i\geq 0$, which has
density $1/2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1136.variants.mueller :
    AvoidsPowersOfTwo muellerSet ∧ muellerSet.HasDensity (1 / 2) := by
  sorry

/--
Müller also proved this is best possible, in that $A$ with the property in the question has
lower density at most $1/2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1136.variants.upper_bound (A : Set ℕ) (hA : AvoidsPowersOfTwo A) :
    A.lowerDensity ≤ 1 / 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos1136

sources_consulted: Erich Härtter’s zbMATH review of Müller, Über ein additiv-zahlentheoretisches Problem von P. Erdős, Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamb. 30 (2011), 75–78; Zbl 1283.11054. Read through https://api.zbmath.org/v1/document/_search?search_string=additiv-zahlentheoretisches
https://www.mathges.hamburg/Download/Zeitschriften/Band30.pdf — contents page only, not the full article
could_not_verify: Erdos1136.erdos_1136 — Could not directly verify that the original question uses precisely lower density strictly greater than 1/3. The cited erdosproblems.com page and forum returned Cloudflare challenges despite descriptive User-Agent headers. The publisher supplied only a contents page, and the accessible zbMATH review does not quote the original 1/3 threshold. The Lean statement’s semantics and its affirmative answer are supported by the checks and external proof, but exact fidelity of this threshold remains unverified.
review.notes: No mathematical defect was substantiated. Importantly, the zbMATH review explicitly states the optimality bound using lower density (liminf), supporting variants.upper_bound; the stronger upper-density bound in the external proof is not evidence of a misformalization. Lean scratch checks confirmed the density definitions, zero/empty cases, avoidance by multiples of three, and the equivalence n ∈ muellerSet ↔ ∃ i q, n = 2^i * (4*q+3). Exact bounded-membership computations also passed. The cited external proof compiled through main_result after adding [Pi.neg_def] to one simp call for toolchain compatibility; its axioms were only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Its counting convention differs by at most one endpoint, leaving density unchanged, so it supports the affirmative answer and formal_proof record. The accessible status database records the problem as proved in Lean. Source-access limitations prevent an unqualified conclusion about the original question’s precise wording.
